beginner.title: Understand RAG without getting lost in the machinery.
beginner.description: Start with the open-book analogy, follow one small example, and learn why evidence matters before an answer is written.
beginner.prerequisite: No AI background or coding is required.
outcomes: Explain retrieval, augmentation and generation in everyday language.
Trace a question to a supporting source sentence.
Recognize when the documents do not support an answer.
practice: Write three fictional policy sentences and underline the one that answers a question.
Use the architecture buttons to explain the difference between preparing documents and answering a question.
readiness: I can explain why a fluent answer can still be unsupported.
I can distinguish the document collection, the retriever and the answer-writing model.

intermediate.title: Compare the choices inside a retrieval pipeline.
intermediate.description: Move from the idea to chunks, embeddings, stores, retrieval methods and measurable results. Use the workbenches to see what changes.
intermediate.prerequisite: You understand the three RAG stages and why source evidence matters; start with Beginner if these are new.
outcomes: Compare chunking strategies and explain overlap.
Distinguish a vector database, similarity measure and search index.
Calculate precision and recall with explicit denominators.
practice: Change window size and overlap, and explain which chunks keep the approval condition intact.
Compare keyword, toy-vector and hybrid rankings for the same question; describe one tradeoff.
readiness: I can explain when exact wording and semantic matching help differently.
I can separate retrieval quality from answer correctness and identify a useful baseline.

advanced.title: Design and evaluate a dependable RAG system.
advanced.description: Reason about architecture, index versions, access boundaries, controlled experiments and operational tradeoffs.
advanced.prerequisite: You can compare retrieval configurations and explain evaluation metrics; complete Intermediate first if needed.
outcomes: Design a versioned chunk/index contract with update and deletion behavior.
Diagnose failures by pipeline stage instead of adding complexity blindly.
Plan a held-out comparison with resource constraints and rollback criteria.
practice: Specify an index migration that keeps embedding versions separate and preserves source traceability.
Design a two-by-two chunking/retrieval experiment and state what evidence would justify rollout.
readiness: I can distinguish relevance, authorization, grounding and operational performance.
I can defend a design decision using measured evidence and explain what remains untested.

beginner.title: Understand what MCP connects and who does what.
beginner.description: Use the reception-desk analogy and diagrams to separate the model, host, client, server and underlying system.
beginner.prerequisite: No programming experience is required. RAG is optional background.
outcomes: Define MCP as a protocol rather than a model or database.
Distinguish tools, resources and reusable prompts.
Explain how MCP and RAG can work together without being the same thing.
practice: Trace a request for a fictional report through host, client, server and data source.
Give one example each of a tool, a resource and a prompt template.
readiness: I can explain why connecting a server does not automatically grant access to everything.
I can describe a useful MCP capability without calling it a language model.

intermediate.title: Follow requests and design a clear tool contract.
intermediate.description: Explore request/result behavior, local and remote transports, protocol compatibility and narrow input contracts.
intermediate.prerequisite: You understand host/client/server roles and the three building blocks; use Beginner first if needed.
outcomes: Distinguish a tool call, a resource read and a prompt request.
Explain schema validation separately from authorization.
Recognize version-sensitive examples and different failure modes.
practice: Run the simulator for a successful call, denied request, unknown dataset and unavailable server.
Write valid and invalid argument objects for the fictional quality-summary schema.
readiness: I can say which component stopped a failed request and whether execution was reached.
I can explain why an argument schema and a protocol connection are not access-control policies.

advanced.title: Reason about production boundaries and compatibility.
advanced.description: Consider identity, delegation, side effects, retries, observability and regression testing before connecting consequential operations.
advanced.prerequisite: You can follow the request flow and design a narrow contract; complete Intermediate before this design review.
outcomes: Identify host, server and downstream authorization boundaries.
Explain why retries, timeouts and cancellation need operation-specific handling.
Separate protocol compatibility, business correctness and model interpretation in a test plan.
practice: Design a safe operating contract for a hypothetical issue-creation tool, including duplicate handling.
Write a regression matrix for two identities, a transport failure, invalid input and an SDK/protocol migration.
readiness: I can explain why a timeout does not prove an operation was rolled back.
I can identify the guarantees a browser simulation cannot establish about a real integration.
